enrichment.short_title: Court refused late production of underwriter correspondence on appeal
key_facts: On the eve of a Court of Appeal hearing, Somatra's solicitors (SRT) applied for an order requiring HFW/Arig to produce correspondence from March–April 1994 relating to Mr Domingo's settlement authority in the underlying ABT Summer insurance action.
Arig offered voluntary limited production on terms including a non-waiver of privilege clause; Somatra opposed, arguing the application was late and breached an October 2001 undertaking.

The court held it had no jurisdiction to order production against Arig's consent and that ordering privileged documents would be inappropriate where the request was solicitor-initiated rather than court-initiated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application during a pending Court of Appeal hearing concerning document production.
enrichment.outcome: Application for production refused; reasons given separately from the refusal announced on the first day of the appeal.
enrichment.ratio: On an appeal where privilege is claimed, the Court of Appeal should not order production of further privileged documents unless the holder consents on agreed terms; it cannot compel production over a privilege claim or order that production does not waive privilege, and a late solicitor-initiated request is not equivalent to the court itself requiring documents.
legal_issues: Whether the Court of Appeal could order production of privileged underwriter correspondence
Whether late production would breach prior undertakings and waive privilege
Whether production on Arig's conditional terms was appropriate

enrichment.short_title: Council did not set too high a hurdle to reject Inspector on Ermine Street

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Development Plan) (England) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Fairfield Partnership challenged Huntingdonshire District Council's adoption of a Local Plan Alteration allocating Ermine Street, Huntingdon for housing, seeking instead allocation of Cardinal Park.
An Inspector had recommended Ermine Street for housing; after consultation the Council resolved not to propose further modifications and to adopt the Alteration.
Fairfield argued officers and legal advice over-circumscribed councillors by treating Inspector recommendations as binding unless 'very good reasons' or new evidence existed to depart from them.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under section 287 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to quash all or part of a local plan alteration.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the Council was not shown to have applied an unlawfully stringent test when deciding not to delete the Ermine Street allocation.
enrichment.ratio: When considering objections to proposed local plan modifications, a planning authority must give reasons sufficient to show whether a section 287 challenge is reasonably arguable; for matters of planning judgment it need not prove the Inspector wrong or its reasons objectively superior, and requiring no more than relevant planning reasons before departing from an Inspector's recommendation is not an error of law if members genuinely understood they could depart on that basis.
legal_issues: The legal test for a council choosing not to follow an Inspector's local plan recommendation
Whether officers' and legal advice set too high a hurdle ('adequate reasons', 'very good reasons', need for new evidence)
Whether the Council's November 2002 resolution showed it felt legally unable to challenge the Inspector
Whether Fairfield was a person aggrieved under section 287(1)

enrichment.short_title: Bankrupt had no standing; costs compromise excluded untaxed sum
key_facts: Boyd & Hutchinson sought to enforce £5,333.57 costs taxed in 1998 against Mr Foenander; he argued a 22 November 1999 compromise discharged the liability.

The compromise letter related to enforcement of a charging order securing about £6,928.78 and scheduled £6,900 in instalments, stating payment would discharge all liabilities including costs in those proceedings.
After permission to appeal was granted, Foenander was adjudicated bankrupt; the trustee did not pursue the appeal.

enrichment.outcome: Adjournment refused; appeal dismissed for want of standing; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused; costs on indemnity basis.
enrichment.ratio: A bankrupt has no standing to pursue an appeal to resist enforcement of a provable debt where the relevant property has vested in the trustee; and on construction of a compromise letter addressed to charging-order enforcement proceedings, a known but unmentioned separately taxed costs sum was not within the parties' intended scope of discharge.

Whether the 22 November 1999 compromise included costs taxed on 7 September 1998

enrichment.short_title: Solicitors' negligence cost Somatra 75% insurance settlement
key_facts: Somatra claimed on insurers after the VLCC ABT Summer exploded and sank in 1991; Sinclair Roche & Temperley (SRT) acted but Somatra lost trust after admitted breaches including misleading instructions to Norwegian law expert Professor Bull.

On the eve of trial in April 1994 Somatra took over negotiations and settled at two-thirds of the claim; the judge found that but for SRT's breaches a 75% settlement would have been offered by underwriter representative Mr Domingo and accepted.
SRT appealed on causation and challenged findings that Mr Domingo had authority to settle at 75%; the Court of Appeal upheld the judge's assessment of Mr Domingo and dismissed the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against High Court judgment awarding Somatra the difference between a two-thirds settlement and the 75% settlement it would have achieved but for solicitors' negligence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; subsidiary rulings included standard-basis costs on the appeal and on a late document-production application.
enrichment.ratio: Where a solicitor's breaches foreseeably destroy a client's trust and confidence, causing the client to settle an insurance claim for less than would otherwise have been obtained, loss is recoverable if the trial judge's findings on the counterfactual settlement figure and the underwriter representative's authority are open on the evidence; an appellate court will not overturn such credibility findings without hearing the witness.

Whether Mr Domingo had authority to offer a 75% settlement

enrichment.short_title: Colliery officials' flexible hours not capped at 40 per week
key_facts: NACODS members employed as colliery officials by UK Coal challenged rostering requiring regular weekend work beyond a perceived 40-hour limit.
Contracts incorporated the 'Ways of Working' collective agreement negotiated after Barber v RJB Mining on working time, providing flexible hours tied to operational needs.
Both sides understood hours would reduce over time, but no fixed maximum hour cap was written into the agreement; grievance procedures addressed unreasonable hours.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court claim for declaratory/construction relief on the contractual working hours of officials.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for the defendant; officials are not contractually limited to 40 hours per week, subject to reasonableness, safety, consultation and grievance procedures.
enrichment.ratio: Where a collective agreement and statutory statement provide for 'flexible' hours to meet reasonable operational and business needs, reference to a 'normal working week of 40 hours' sets a basic framework rather than a contractual maximum; obligations to work according to business need, roster equitably, and challenge unreasonable hours through grievance procedures show the parties intended a non-fixed-hours regime restrained by reasonableness not a 40-hour cap.
legal_issues: Whether 'normal working week of 40 hours' is a contractual maximum or descriptive baseline
Effect of flexibility, mobility and shift-change provisions in the collective agreement
Admissibility of negotiation history and questionnaires in construing employment contracts
Application of Glendale Managed Services v Graham to 'normal' working hours

enrichment.short_title: No conditional restoration power did not breach A1P1

statutes_considered.title: Nurses, Midwives and Health Visitors Act 1979
Nurses, Midwives and Health Visitors Act 1997

key_facts: Miss Hamilton, a nurse and midwife with bi-polar affective disorder, was suspended on health grounds in 1999; the Health Committee refused to terminate suspension in December 2001.
The Professional Conduct Rules (1993 SI 893) rule 49 allowed only termination or continuation of suspension, with no express power for conditional restoration.
Expert evidence showed she was currently well but at risk of relapse without psychiatric follow-up; she argued the either/or scheme violated Article 1 Protocol 1 ECHR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated/judicial review against refusal to terminate suspension; permission granted only on A1P1 conditional restoration issue.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; existing rule 49 scheme held compatible with Article 1 Protocol 1; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Registration as a nurse may be treated as a possession for A1P1 purposes, but an either/or power to terminate or continue health suspension is not a disproportionate interference where the committee may adjourn, give reasons indicating what is required before reapplication, and terminate suspension once adequate monitoring arrangements exist; absence of express conditional restoration is not an excessive burden violating the First Protocol.
legal_issues: Whether rule 49 implicitly permits conditional termination of suspension
Whether nursing registration is a 'possession' under Article 1 Protocol 1
Whether the either/or suspension scheme violates A1P1
Whether Miss Hamilton lost nothing because conditional restoration was not realistically available on the evidence

enrichment.short_title: SGS and bank liable in lead fraud letter-of-credit case
key_facts: Niru contracted to buy lead from Milestone (controlled by Mr Mahdavi); Bank Sepah opened a letter of credit requiring SGS inspection certificates and bills of lading.
Mahdavi procured false documents including an SGS certificate and bills of lading for goods not properly loaded; Bank Sepah paid under the credit and CAI received and paid away funds.

enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; SGS liable for breach of duty; CAI liable in restitution; CAI acquitted of deceit upheld; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: SGS owed Niru a duty of care in issuing inspection certificates under the letter of credit and was liable for breach; CAI was not liable in deceit where dishonesty was not proved, but restitution of mistaken payments is not defeated by a change-of-position defence where it would be inequitable and unconscionable to allow the recipient to retain funds—negligence or bad faith short of dishonesty may suffice, and dishonesty is not a universal prerequisite to defeat change of position.

enrichment.short_title: No power to redact customer data from registered charge forms
key_facts: igroup and subsidiary mortgage lenders delivered forms 395 and 403b to the Registrar with schedules containing accurate customer mortgage details (names, balances, rates) beyond what was strictly required.

The Registrar entered correct particulars on the Register of Charges and retained the forms as public records; igroup sought removal or replacement of the schedules to protect customer confidentiality.
The Registrar opposed; no breach of confidence, data protection or Article 8 by the Registrar was established.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim for rectification or amendment of filed charge forms and schedules.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no jurisdiction under section 404 or inherent jurisdiction to amend the forms or schedules.
enrichment.ratio: Section 404 empowers rectification only of omissions or misstatements in particulars entered on the Register of Charges or memoranda of satisfaction, not in forms filed with the Registrar; accurate but excessive disclosure in filed forms is not a 'misstatement', and Exeter Trust v Screenways excludes inherent rectification power where the statutory scheme is exhaustive; the Registrar must retain filed documents for public inspection.
legal_issues: Whether section 404 extends to forms 395/403b and attached schedules
Whether inclusion of accurate unnecessary personal data is a misstatement
Whether the court has inherent jurisdiction to order the Registrar to amend filed documents
Whether disclosure breached duties of confidence, the Data Protection Act 1998 or Article 8 ECHR

key_facts: Hoar-Stevens faced drink-driving proceedings relying on EC/1R intoximeter readings; the defence sought stay for inadequate disclosure of machine reliability material from Intoximeters and the Home Office.

enrichment.ratio: The Divisional Court has no jurisdiction to quash or control interlocutory decisions of magistrates while summary trial is incomplete; Buck v Rochford Justices remains good law, and even important disclosure issues must ordinarily be resolved after the magistrates' court proceedings end, not by mid-trial judicial review or declaration.

enrichment.short_title: Gypsy status retained despite lack of travelling sites

statutes_considered.title: Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960

key_facts: The Coopers, ethnic Romany Gypsies, sought planning permission for a caravan site at Fanton Hall Cottages, Essex; Basildon District Council refused.
The Secretary of State allowed the appeal; the council challenged on section 288 grounds arguing the Coopers had abandoned nomadic life.

The inspector found the family wished to travel but were forced onto the site by lack of temporary stopping places, ill health and children's needs; the Secretary of State conceded the challenge might succeed but the Coopers defended the decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 appeal against Secretary of State decision granting planning permission for change of use to a Gypsy caravan site.
enrichment.outcome: Council's appeal dismissed; inspector's decision and grant of permission upheld; costs ordered against the council.
enrichment.ratio: Applying Wrexham, Gypsy status depends on whether persons of nomadic habit of life have abandoned that way of life as a matter of fact and degree; inability to travel because of lack of sites, together with an honest intention to resume travelling and continued caravan living without seeking permanent housing, can support retention of Gypsy status even when not currently travelling.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector failed to take relevant matters into account on Gypsy status
Whether lack of temporary sites can explain cessation of travelling without loss of status
Whether the inspector erred in law or gave inadequate reasons
